analysis.one_liner: Makes some bankruptcy filers repay part of their debts and gives debtors new penalties against abusive creditors.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bankruptcy overhaul 97-1 in September 1998, but the House never voted on the Senate version before Congress ended, so no bankruptcy law changed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make bankruptcy 'needs-based': a court could dismiss a Chapter 7 liquidation case and move the person into a Chapter 3-year repayment plan if their income could cover at least a fifth of their unsecured debts, while shielding below-median-income families from such motions. It would also give debtors new tools to recover money from creditors who inflate claims, ignore court protections, or made predatory loans, require credit counseling before filing, put child support first in line for repayment, and tighten paperwork deadlines and audits. Both chambers passed versions of this overhaul in 1998, but they never reconciled them.
analysis.who_benefits: Creditors gain when higher-income debtors are pushed into repayment plans instead of erasing debts. Debtors gain fee awards and damages against creditors who file inflated claims, violate automatic stays, or made predatory loans. Single parents and children owed support move to the front of the bankruptcy payment line.

how_it_helps.text: A debtor whose household income is at or below the national median is protected from any motion to dismiss their Chapter 7 case, so most working families keep access to liquidation.

Debtors can recover attorneys' fees, and in some cases damages, from creditors who file inflated or unsupported claims, refuse reasonable repayment negotiations, or willfully violate the automatic stay that stops collections.
Claims based on loans that violated the Truth in Lending Act's high-cost mortgage disclosure rules are disallowed, so predatory lenders cannot enforce them in bankruptcy.
Child and spousal support claims get first priority in bankruptcy, support arrears can be enforced despite the automatic stay, and discharge is conditioned on keeping up support payments.
Debts from drunk-driving crashes involving boats or aircraft become nondischargeable, and debts run up shortly before filing are presumed not dischargeable.

analysis.who_pays: Debtors with above-median income who can repay at least 20% of their unsecured debts lose the clean-slate liquidation and must fund multi-year repayment plans. All filers face a credit counseling requirement, random audits of their petitions, faster automatic-dismissal deadlines for missing paperwork, and smaller homestead exemption limits for expensive homes, and debtors' lawyers face personal fee liability that can raise the cost of filing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Higher-income debtors seeking a fresh start

drawbacks.text: The needs-based standard repeals the presumption in favor of granting the relief a debtor requests and lets a court convert a liquidation to a repayment plan even without the debtor's consent, narrowing the fresh start for households judged able to repay a fifth of their unsecured debts.
Every filer must attempt a credit counseling repayment plan and complete a financial-management course before receiving a discharge, adding cost and delay for people already in financial distress.
Debtors' attorneys must reimburse trustees' legal fees and face civil penalties if a court finds a filing unjustified, which raises the price and risk of legal representation for struggling families.
Liens are retained until the underlying debt is fully paid and secured claims are redefined more favorably to lenders, reducing what Chapter 13 debtors can strip down.
The homestead exemption is capped at $100,000 in certain home and burial-plot equity, limiting what families in high-cost states can shield from creditors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine compromise bill, not a giveaway. Debtors below the median income keep full access to liquidation and gain real new penalties against creditor abuse, including on predatory loans. The trade-off is that higher-income debtors who once could wipe out unsecured debts would be pushed into repayment, and everyone faces counseling requirements, audits, and stricter paperwork deadlines that add cost and risk of dismissal. Critics on the debtor side considered the means test too broad and the counseling requirement a hurdle; critics on the creditor side considered the new fee-shifting and damages provisions too punishing for lenders. Both sides gave up something real.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the overhaul 97-1 as an amendment to the House's companion bankruptcy bill, but the House never voted on the Senate's version before the 105th Congress ended, so nothing became law.

narrative.text: Grassley introduced the bill for himself and Senator Durbin on October 21, 1997, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.

After hearings and a subcommittee vote, the Judiciary Committee reported the bill on June 4, 1998 with a substitute amendment, and it was placed on the Senate calendar; minority views were filed with the committee report.
The Senate took the bill up in September 1998; a procedural vote to move forward passed 99-1, with all 45 Democrats and 54 of 55 Republicans in favor.
After days of floor debate, the Senate incorporated the bill into H.R. 3150 as an amendment and passed the companion House bill in its place by 97-1 on September 23, 1998.
No further action appears in the record; the House never took up the Senate's version, and the 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999 without a bankruptcy law change.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No side fully won. Debtors kept the old bankruptcy rules — including unrestricted Chapter 7 access and no counseling mandate — while creditors avoided the new fee-shifting and damages penalties but also failed, after years of pressing, to get the repayment standards enacted in this Congress. The fight simply carried into future Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly unanimous across parties: the vote to take the bill up was 99-1 (all 45 Democrats and 54 of 55 Republicans), and final passage was 97-1 (54 of 55 Republicans, 43 of 45 Democrats).

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: The needs-based standard and the presumption against recently incurred luxury debts push more debtors into repayment plans and shrink what can be erased, so lenders collect on debts that would otherwise be discharged. That gain comes directly out of debtors' fresh start.

industries.industry: Secured lenders (auto, retail installment, and mortgage creditors)
industries.note: The bill lets lienholders retain their liens until debts are fully paid, strengthens secured-claim status, and speeds relief from the automatic stay, so these creditors recover more from bankruptcy estates at debtors' expense.
The bill requires every bankruptcy filer to attempt a repayment plan through an approved counseling program before filing, making these agencies a mandatory gateway to the bankruptcy courts.

Claims based on loans that violated the Truth in Lending Act's high-cost loan disclosure rules would be disallowed in bankruptcy, hitting lenders whose gains come from loans the law already treats as abusive.

Debtors' lawyers face reimbursing trustees' fees and civil penalties if a court finds a filing unjustified, raising their risk, but they also gain fee awards when they defeat creditor motions and inflated claims.
